leads.extracted_text: Viruses and bacteria are two of the most common microorganisms that cause diseases, but they are very different from each other. Both can lead to infections, yet they vary in their size, structure, how they live, and the way they spread. Bacteria are complete living cells that can survive on their own, while viruses can multiply only inside a living host. Understanding these differences is important for identifying the right treatment and for knowing how various infections develop. Lysogeny is characterized by integration of the bacteriophage nucleic acid into the host bacterium's genome or formation of a circular replicon in the bacterial cytoplasm. In this condition the bacterium continues to live and reproduce normally, while the bacteriophage lies in a dormant state in the host cell. Viruses are the smallest and simplest life form known. They are 10 to 100 times smaller than bacteria.

The biggest difference between viruses and bacteria is that viruses must have a living host - like a plant or animal - to multiply, while most bacteria can grow on non-living surfaces.

Bacteria are intercellular organisms (i.e. they live in-between cells); whereas viruses are intracellular organisms (they infiltrate the host cell and live inside the cell). They change the host cell's genetic material from its normal function to producing the virus itself.

Rapid and effective testing is imperative, so we can successfully treat the offending microorganism.

Cell vs particle. A bacterium is a complete cell; a virus is not. Almost every difference follows from this.

Both for the cell, one for the particle. A bacterium has DNA and RNA; a virus genome is DNA or RNA.

Big bug, small bug. Bacteria are measured in micrometers and seen with a light microscope; viruses in nanometers, needing an electron microscope.

No target, no effect. Antibiotics hit bacterial structures (cell wall, ribosomes) that viruses do not have.
